reproduction_target: Pipeline-executability readiness of RawBench, a modular Nextflow + C++ benchmarking framework for raw nanopore signal analysis (RSA). The shipped pipeline decomposes RSA into three stages and evaluates thirty pipeline combinations across four datasets (E. coli, D. melanogaster, H. sapiens, Zymo mock metagenome; R9.4.1 and R10.4.1 chemistries): stage 1 reference-genome encoding with k-mer pore models (ONT vs Uncalled4 learned model); stage 2 raw-signal segmentation (t-test changepoint detection, Dorado move tables, Campolina CNN); stage 3 representation matching (hash-based / RawHash2, FM-index / UNCALLED, vector distances / Sigmap, R-index / Sigmoni-SPUMONI, DTW / RawAlign) for read mapping and read classification; plus RSA-assisted basecalling (pre-basecalling filtering and Dorado context-length limiting to 1/2/5/10 chunks of 4000 signal points), ground truth generation via Dorado super-accurate (SUP) basecalling followed by minimap2, quality scoring with UNCALLED pafstats (TP/FP/FN/NA, precision, recall, F1), and performance measurement (elapsed time, CPU time, peak memory) on a fixed server (NVIDIA A6000 GPU, Intel Xeon Gold 6226R, 64 threads). There is no wet-lab component in this study: all nanopore data are pre-existing public datasets, so W = 0 and every enumerated step is computational.
granularity_note: Coarse one-step-per-named-tool/analysis, built from the bioRxiv v1 JATS source XML. FETCH NOTE: WebFetch of https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2025/10/06/2025.10.04.680405.source.xml returned HTTP 403; a direct curl with a browser User-Agent returned HTTP 200 / 196,525 bytes. The fetch was written into an isolated per-paper scratch directory (/tmp/stage1_10.1101_2025.10.04.680405/paper.xml) and article identity was verified BEFORE scoring by grepping the title token 'Comprehensive Benchmarking Framework for Raw Nanopore' and the DOI string '10.1101/2025.10.04.680405' in the fetched bytes; both matched, so no swap occurred. ROUTING: this is a boundary case between 'tool-methods' and 'hybrid'. It is routed tool-methods because the deliverable is the shipped framework and the reported Tables 2-9 are that framework's own output; under the guide's tool-methods rule the metric is PIPELINE EXECUTABILITY READINESS (not 'reproducibility') and the denominator is pipeline steps only, which is exactly the 19-step list below. A human reviewer may re-route to hybrid and dual-score; that would not change the axes, only the label. MATERIAL EVIDENCE LIMITATION: the two artifacts that carry all parameter and version evidence - Supplementary Table S7 ('Parameters we use in our evaluation for each tool and dataset in mapping', including preset values) and Supplementary Table S8 ('Versions of each tool and library', stated to give 'the version and the link to these corresponding versions of each tool we use in our experiments') - exist in the JATS only as graphic references (680405v1_tblS7, 680405v1_tblS8); the XML contains ZERO <table> elements, so no table body could be read. Scoring therefore credits the CLAIM that per-tool exact versions and per-tool/per-dataset parameters are tabulated (version = 1, params = 2 for tool invocations) but cannot verify their content. Table 1, which the prose says carries the dataset names 'as hypertexts referring to the source', is likewise a graphic; consequently NO dataset accession identifier is readable anywhere in the article text. VERSION CEILING: version is capped at 1 for every step - exact pins without environment closure (subflag exact_pins_partial). This is not merely the Stage-1 ceiling: the repository landing page and DEPENDENCIES.md were read and neither ships a lockfile, conda environment.yml, requirements.txt, Dockerfile nor Singularity definition; conda environments are named only ('sigmoni', 'mm2', 'bamtofastq') with install instructions in prose, external tools (Dorado, RawHash2) must be installed separately and located via DORADO_PATH / RAWHASH2_PATH, and SPUMONI is built from a git submodule with cmake. The paper cites the repository as a bare URL with no release tag, commit hash, or Zenodo DOI. CODE AXIS: code = 2 for steps whose implementation is the RawBench repository itself or a public third-party tool wrapped by it (the repo is public, MIT-licensed, and states 'Scripts to reproduce each of the experiments can be found on https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/RawBench'); code = 1 only for Campolina, whose pretrained CNN weights are not mentioned in the paper prose or the repository landing page and which the paper itself describes as 'requiring extensive pretraining'. DATA AXIS: data = 2 throughout - all four datasets are pre-existing public nanopore datasets, Table 1 states they are hyperlinked to source, preprocessing scripts are said to be provided, and the repository landing page documents 'cd refs && bash download_refs.sh' and 'cd fast5 && bash download.sh'. The one NI step is C1: no reference genome assembly build/version is stated anywhere in the retrievable prose, which is an unknown-version condition (version = 0), not a floating-version condition. Whether download_refs.sh pins versioned URLs is precisely the Stage-2 env_capture_class A/B/C question and is deliberately left n/a here.

steps.label: Reference genome acquisition and preparation for E. coli, D. melanogaster, H. sapiens and the Zymo mock community (repository landing page: 'cd refs && bash download_refs.sh'); no assembly build or accession stated in the retrievable prose

Raw nanopore signal dataset acquisition and preprocessing (FAST5/POD5 raw signals plus basecalled FASTQ; R9.4.1 and R10.4.1 chemistries, 400 bps preferred over deprecated 260 bps; Table 1 dataset names stated to hyperlink to source; repository landing page: 'cd fast5 && bash download.sh')
Stage 1 reference encoding with the official ONT k-mer pore model (translating reference genome into expected electrical signal patterns)
Stage 1 reference encoding with the Uncalled4 de-novo-learned k-mer pore model (repository ships kmer_models/, e.g. uncalled4_r10.4.1.txt)
Stage 2 signal segmentation by t-test changepoint detection (standalone RawBench C++ module; default segmentation for all non-segmentation experiments)
Stage 2 signal segmentation from basecaller move tables (Dorado intermediate output used as coarse segmentation points)

Stage 2 signal segmentation with Campolina, a CNN trained to predict segmentation points; paper states it requires extensive pretraining, and no pretrained weights or training recipe are described in prose or on the repository landing page

Stage 3 hash-based matching (quantization into shared hash buckets; RawHash/RawHash2 family; default matching method for read mapping and RSA-assisted basecalling). Installed separately as a prebuilt binary via ../bin/rawhash2 or RAWHASH2_PATH
Stage 3 FM-index matching (UNCALLED probabilistic FM-index estimating signal-to-k-mer match likelihood)
Stage 3 vector-distance matching (Sigmap-style embedding of signal and reference into a shared high-dimensional space)
Stage 3 R-index matching computing pseudo-matching lengths (Sigmoni over the SPUMONI backend, built from spumoni_submodule via cmake; default matching method for read classification)
Stage 3 Dynamic Time Warping matching, including the RawAlign-style hybrid of fast seeding plus selective DTW refinement

Ground-truth basecalling with Dorado super-accurate (SUP) model, GPU-accelerated, using the model matched to the data sampling frequency (4 kHz or 5 kHz); installed separately and located via DORADO_PATH
Ground-truth read mapping with minimap2 (identical parameter setting for all datasets per Appendix C.1; installed in a dedicated 'mm2' conda environment)
RSA-assisted basecalling: pre-basecalling raw-signal filtering, comparing depth of coverage with and without limiting Dorado to reads successfully mapped by RSA
Basecaller context-length sweep: limiting Dorado context to 1, 2, 5 or 10 chunks of 4000 signal points each (approximately 1 second of data)

Quality metric computation with UNCALLED pafstats: TP, FP, FN, NA, precision, recall and F1 against the Dorado-SUP-plus-minimap2 ground truth; BAM/FASTQ conversion via the 'bamtofastq' conda environment

Performance measurement: elapsed wall-clock time, CPU time and peak memory, 64 threads for all CPU workloads, GPU used only for Dorado, on a single stated server (NVIDIA A6000, Intel Xeon Gold 6226R at 2.90 GHz)

Nextflow orchestration of the modular framework: composition and execution of the thirty RSA pipeline combinations drawn from the RawBench component pool, plus wrapper scripts invoking prebuilt binaries of established RSA tools (nextflow-pipeline/, job_scripts/, scripts/setup_env.sh with validate_environment)

headline.static_readiness: 0/19 (0%) - stage1 ceiling only, no R-star (R-star needs stage-2 code verification)
headline.inference_inclusive_upper_bound: 18/19 (95%) RI, 1/19 (5%) NI. This is an unusually strong Stage-1 profile for pipeline-executability readiness, and the binding constraint is a single one: environment closure. On the positive side, every axis except Version has real support. Code: the framework is public and MIT-licensed at https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/RawBench, the paper states twice that the datasets, evaluation scripts and documentation live there ('Scripts to reproduce each of the experiments can be found on ...'), the landing page documents a recursive clone, a cmake build of the SPUMONI submodule, conda environment creation, reference and signal download scripts, and a 'source scripts/setup_env.sh && validate_environment' entry point. Data: all four datasets (E. coli, D. melanogaster, H. sapiens, Zymo mock) are pre-existing public nanopore data with download scripts shipped, so no step is blocked by an embargo and W = 0. Params: the paper explicitly tabulates per-tool, per-dataset parameters including presets (Supplementary Table S7) and states the thread count (64) and the GPU/CPU split. Version is where it stops. The paper claims Supplementary Table S8 gives 'the version and the link to these corresponding versions of each tool', which is exactly the exact_pins_partial pattern: scattered exact pins with no interpreter pin, no channel/index pin, no declared platform. The repository confirms this from the other side - DEPENDENCIES.md names conda environments ('sigmoni', 'mm2', 'bamtofastq') but ships no environment.yml, no conda-lock, no requirements.txt, no Dockerfile and no Singularity definition, and Dorado and RawHash2 are prebuilt binaries located through DORADO_PATH / RAWHASH2_PATH. There is also no release tag, commit hash or Zenodo DOI for the framework itself, so 'the code' names a moving branch. Consequently version = 1 everywhere and no step can exceed RI even under a successful Stage-2 code check. The single NI step is C1 (reference genome preparation): no assembly build or accession is stated in any retrievable prose, an unknown-version rather than a floating-version condition. Two further limits on this number, stated symmetrically: (a) it UNDER-claims nothing on the code side but OVER-claims nothing either - params = 2 and version = 1 rest on the CLAIMED content of Supplementary Tables S7 and S8, whose bodies are graphics in the JATS and could not be read; (b) the runtime and peak-memory results (Tables 4-9, S3-S6) are bound to one specific server (A6000 GPU, Xeon Gold 6226R, 64 threads) and are by construction not reproducible on different hardware, which this rubric's four axes do not penalise.
headline.coverage: 19/19 computational steps (100%); W = 0. Steps were enumerated from Sections 3.1-3.4 (the three RSA stages plus RSA-assisted basecalled analysis), Section 4 (datasets), Section 5.1 (Evaluation Methodology, Methods and Experimental Setup) and Appendix C (Configuration) of the bioRxiv v1 JATS source XML, one step per named tool or analysis invocation: 1 reference-genome preparation, 1 dataset acquisition/preprocessing, 2 pore-model reference-encoding variants, 3 segmentation variants, 5 matching variants, 2 ground-truth steps (Dorado SUP, minimap2), 2 RSA-assisted-basecalling experiments, 1 quality-metric step (UNCALLED pafstats), 1 performance-measurement step, 1 Nextflow orchestration step. There is no wet-lab work in this paper - all nanopore signals are pre-existing public data - so the computational coverage is complete and no OOS split was required. The thirty pipeline combinations reported in the paper are the cross-product of the component steps and are represented once, as C19, rather than expanded into thirty steps; expanding them would inflate every ratio without adding evidence, since each combination inherits the axes of its components.

gaps.where: Gap subtype 2a (version not recorded at the environment level). Environment closure and framework versioning - all 19 computational steps
gaps.missing: No environment lock of any kind is claimed by the paper or by the repository landing page. The paper's only version evidence is Appendix C.2: 'Supplementary Table S8 shows the version and the link to these corresponding versions of each tool we use in our experiments' - scattered exact pins with no interpreter version, no conda channel or package index, and no declared platform, which is the exact_pins_partial pattern (version = 1 by the symmetric env-closure gate, never 2). The repository confirms the absence from the other direction: DEPENDENCIES.md names three conda environments ('sigmoni', 'mm2', 'bamtofastq') and Python 3.8 with h5py/numpy/scipy/ont-fast5-api/uncalled4 for Sigmoni, but ships no environment.yml, no conda-lock.yml, no requirements.txt, no Dockerfile and no Singularity definition. Separately, RawBench itself is cited as a bare branch URL (https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/RawBench) with no release tag, no commit hash and no Zenodo DOI, so the identity of 'the code that produced Tables 2-9' is not fixed in time; the two git submodules (spumoni_submodule, sigmoni_submodule) are pinned by the superproject only if the recorded submodule commits are intact, which is a Stage-2 check.
gaps.how_to_close: Ship a conda-lock or pixi.lock for the declared platform (linux-64) covering the Python and C++ toolchain, or a container with a recorded digest, and pin the interpreter and the channels rather than only package names. Tag a release for the manuscript state of the framework and archive it to Zenodo, then cite the tag/DOI in Section 6 (Resources) and Appendix C.2 instead of the bare repository URL. Record the submodule commit hashes explicitly in DEPENDENCIES.md so a reader can verify them without a working clone.

gaps.where: Section 4 (RawBench Datasets) / Table 1, and Appendix C (Tables S7 and S8) - affects C1, C2 and the parameter/version basis of C3-C19
gaps.missing: No dataset accession identifier appears anywhere in the article text. The prose says only 'Dataset names in Table 1 are provided as hypertexts referring to the source and preprocessing scripts are provided in' - Table 1 is a graphic in the JATS (the XML contains zero <table> elements), so the sample-to-source correspondence is unreadable to any text-based or programmatic reader, and no ENA/SRA/PRJ/ERR identifier is recoverable. The same defect blocks the two artifacts that carry all parameter and version evidence: Supplementary Table S7 (parameters per tool and dataset in mapping, with presets) and Supplementary Table S8 (versions and links per tool) are also graphics. Additionally, no reference genome assembly build is stated for any of the four organisms, which is why C1 scores version = 0.
gaps.how_to_close: Quote the accession or persistent identifier of each of the four datasets (and of each reference assembly, e.g. the exact GRCh38 / BDGP6 / E. coli / Zymo reference release) in the running text of Section 4, not only as hyperlinks inside a table image. Provide Tables 1, S7 and S8 as machine-readable supplementary files (TSV or CSV) in addition to the typeset figures, and mirror them in the repository so they can be diffed against the actual invocations.

gaps.where: C1 and C2 - reference genomes, raw signal datasets and k-mer models obtained out of band
gaps.missing: All external reference resources are delivered by shell download scripts documented only on the repository landing page ('cd refs && bash download_refs.sh', 'cd fast5 && bash download.sh') plus a shipped kmer_models/ directory. Whether those scripts fetch versioned, immutable artifacts (class A), consume user-supplied local paths with the version living only in prose (class B), or pull rolling/latest resources (class C) cannot be decided without reading the scripts, which is out of scope at Stage 1. Per the guide, env_capture_class is therefore left n/a for every step and no R-star is awarded. Note that the k-mer model file name observed on the landing page (uncalled4_r10.4.1.txt) encodes a chemistry, not a model version or checksum.
gaps.how_to_close: Make each download script fetch a versioned URL or accession and verify it against a recorded checksum, and print the resolved version into the run log so a reader can confirm what was actually downloaded. State the reference assembly release inside download_refs.sh rather than relying on a URL that may be repointed.

gaps.where: C8, C13 and C19 - externalised sub-pipelines and prebuilt binaries
gaps.missing: The paper states verbatim: 'For completeness, we also provide benchmarking scripts that invoke prebuilt binaries of established RSA tools; while these wrappers facilitate fair, out-of-the-box comparisons, they naturally limit full combinatorial exploration compared to our C++ modules.' The landing page confirms that Dorado and RawHash2 are not vendored but must be installed separately and located through DORADO_PATH and RAWHASH2_PATH, and that SPUMONI is built from a submodule. A reader therefore reconstructs part of the measured stack by hand, and the binaries they obtain are not guaranteed to be the ones the authors measured unless Supplementary Table S8's links are followed exactly.
gaps.how_to_close: Vendor or lock the external binaries: record the exact download URL plus checksum for the Dorado and RawHash2 builds used, and have setup_env.sh verify them rather than merely validate that a path is set. State explicitly, next to each results table, which numbers came from the C++ modules and which from the prebuilt-binary wrappers.

gaps.where: C18 (and, for the timing and memory columns, C3-C17) - hardware-bound results and path-based environment configuration
gaps.missing: All performance results are tied to one machine: 'We perform all experiments on a server equipped with an NVIDIA A6000 GPU and an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 6226R CPU running at 2.90 GHz. We conduct each evaluation with 64 threads.' Elapsed time, CPU time and peak memory (Tables 4-9, S3-S6, including the reported six hours and 265 GB for H. sapiens) cannot be reproduced on different hardware by construction, and the 265 GB peak places a hard floor on the machine a reader needs. Environment configuration is likewise path-based (DORADO_PATH, RAWHASH2_PATH, '../bin/rawhash2', a job_scripts/ directory presumably written for the authors' scheduler) rather than declarative.
gaps.how_to_close: State the minimum RAM, disk and GPU memory required per dataset next to Table 1, and separate the quality tables (portable) from the performance tables (hardware-bound) with an explicit statement that the latter are machine-specific. Replace hardcoded relative binary paths and site-specific job scripts with a Nextflow profile per execution environment so that the pipeline runs unmodified on another cluster.

gaps.where: C6, C13, C15, C16 - Dorado basecalling models
gaps.missing: The paper states that 'Only Bonito and Dorado basecallers support the latest R10.4.1 chemistry, but rely on proprietary training data, limiting adaptability and reproducibility.' The ground truth for every quality number in the paper is produced by Dorado SUP, and the move-table segmentation arm consumes a Dorado internal output. The Dorado code and released model weights are freely downloadable, so re-execution is not blocked and no step is capped at NI for this reason; what is not reproducible is the model itself, i.e. a reader cannot retrain or audit the ground-truth generator. This is recorded as a scope limit on what 'reproduced' can mean here, not as a penalty.
gaps.how_to_close: Nothing is available to the authors beyond what they already did (naming the model class and sampling frequency). Recording the exact Dorado model identifier (for example the full dna_r10.4.1 SUP model name and revision) alongside the version in Supplementary Table S8 would let a reader confirm they hold the identical weights.

gaps.where: C7 (Campolina CNN) and C13/C15/C16 (Dorado neural basecalling)
gaps.missing: No random seed is stated anywhere in the paper, and no statement is made about determinism. The neural components are used in inference mode, where determinism is likely, but GPU basecalling in particular can be non-deterministic across batch sizes and driver versions, and no replicate runs or run-to-run variability are reported for any quality or performance number.
gaps.how_to_close: State explicitly that all runs are single-shot and deterministic in inference, or report run-to-run variability for at least one representative configuration. If any component samples, set and record the seed and show it is consumed.
